opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one of the parts of that work I'm least satisfied with in retrospect. When we built the navigation model, we essentially decided ahead of time where one "event" ended and the next began. So we'd segment an instruction like "walk down the hallway, turn left at the kitchen, and stop by the couch" into chunks, and we'd align those chunks with segments of the trajectory using fairly hand-specified heuristics. That made the learning problem tractable, but it also baked in a lot of assumptions about what the right units of meaning are.

If I were doing it again, I think the main thing I'd want is for those boundaries to be latent, something the model infers jointly with everything else rather than something we impose. There's a nice analogy here to how people learn language. Kids aren't handed a segmentation of the world into events and then told which words go with which pieces. They figure out the segmentation and the mapping at the same time, and each constrains the other. Language tells you where the interesting boundaries in experience are, and the structure of experience tells you how to carve up the language.

Practically, that could look like a few different things. One option is a more explicitly structured latent-variable model, a kind of semi-Markov or hierarchical alignment model where you marginalize over possible segmentations instead of committing to one. That keeps the interpretability and compositionality we cared about while letting the data decide where the joints are. The other option, given where the field has gone, is to start with a big pretrained model that already has some implicit notion of event structure, and then ask whether you can recover or encourage discrete, reusable segments through the training objective, with something like a bottleneck or an auxiliary prediction task.

The other thing I'd reconsider is the assumption that there's a single correct granularity. "Go to the kitchen" is one event at one level of description and a dozen motor actions at another. A lot of the brittleness we saw came from forcing everything onto one level. So I'd want something more hierarchical, where the model can represent "turn left at the kitchen" both as an atomic step and as something that decomposes further when it needs to. That's closer to how instructions actually work, since people move up and down levels of abstraction constantly depending on what they think the listener already knows.

So the short version is: make the boundaries learned rather than given, let them live at multiple levels, and let language and perception jointly supervise each other in discovering them. That's a harder learning problem, but I think it's much closer to the real one.

r001.rationale: The response proposes making event boundaries latent and having the model infer them jointly with the rest of the task, rather than imposing them in advance.

r002.rationale: It does not predict what an attention-based navigation model would discover; it discusses latent segmentation and pretrained models without making that specific claim.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've actually thought about a fair amount since that work. In the original setup, the way we got the sequence of sub-goals was basically by hand: you have the instruction, you have the trajectory, and we assume there's some natural segmentation of the trajectory into chunks that line up with pieces of the instruction. And in practice we were getting those boundaries from annotations, or from fairly heuristic things like "the agent turned here, so that's probably a new segment."

The thing that bothers me about that in hindsight is that it bakes in a particular theory of what an event is. If I say "go down the hall and take the second left," a human doesn't necessarily experience that as two events with a crisp boundary at the turn. The boundaries are a property of how you're describing the behavior, not necessarily of the behavior itself. And once you fix them in advance, the model has no way to tell you that it would have preferred to carve things up differently.

So the first thing I'd do differently is treat the segmentation as latent. You have a sequence of low-level actions, you have the language, and you want to jointly infer both the alignment between words and actions and the places where one sub-goal ends and the next one begins. That's an old idea, it's basically what people did in unsupervised word segmentation or in HMM-style alignment models, and I think there's a very natural version of it here where you marginalize over boundary placements rather than conditioning on them.

The second thing, which I think is more interesting, is that the right boundaries probably aren't even fixed per trajectory. They depend on what you're trying to communicate. If you're giving someone directions, you segment at decision points. If you're explaining why you took a weird route, you segment around the thing that surprised you. So I'd want the event structure to be conditioned on the communicative goal, not just on the geometry of the path.

And then the honest answer is that some of this might just fall out of scale. If you train a model on enough paired language and behavior, it may learn a segmentation implicitly that's better than anything we'd hand-design. But I'm not sure I'd bet on that fully, because the useful thing about explicit boundaries is that they give you a handle for interpretability and for compositional generalization. If the model has a notion of "this is the step where I went through the door," you can reuse that. If it's all smeared across a continuous representation, you lose that, and that was a lot of the point of the project in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response proposes treating segmentation as latent and jointly inferring language-action alignment and sub-goal boundaries, which communicates learning the boundaries as part of the model.

r002.rationale: The response suggests a sufficiently trained model might learn segmentation implicitly, but it does not identify an attention-based navigation model or predict that it would find different boundaries from the original top-down ones.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d want to make those boundaries something the model learns, rather than something we impose on it. When you break a navigation task into events, you’re making a fairly strong assumption about what the meaningful units of behavior are. Is going down a hallway one event? Does turning a corner start a new one? The useful answer might depend on the instruction.

So one approach would be to treat the segmentation as latent and learn it jointly with the mapping from language to actions. The model could decide when it has completed one part of the instruction and needs to move on to another. The challenge is giving it enough structure that those segments actually help it generalize, without prescribing in advance exactly where every boundary should fall.

r001.rationale: It proposes learning event segmentation jointly with the language-to-action mapping, instead of imposing boundaries.

r002.rationale: It does not mention an attention-based navigation model or predict that it would discover different boundaries from the imposed ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the thing you’d really like to do is make those boundaries latent. In the navigation model, we impose a segmentation that says, roughly, this part of the instruction corresponds to this part of the trajectory. That’s a useful simplification, but it’s also a fairly strong assumption about how language and actions line up.

Instead, you could have the model infer both what the relevant events are and where they begin and end, using the instruction and the observations together. The interesting question is whether it discovers segments that correspond to meaningful subgoals—getting to an intersection, making a turn—or just segments that happen to make prediction easier. So I’d want to evaluate whether those learned boundaries actually help the model generalize to new instructions and new environments.

r001.rationale: The response proposes that the model infer the events and their boundaries from the instruction and observations, instead of imposing the segmentation.

r002.rationale: It discusses what learned boundaries might represent, but does not predict that an attention-based model would discover boundaries different from the original top-down ones.
